terms.gloss: go down into the bath, get in
terms.grammar: dēscendō, dēscendere, dēscendī, dēscēnsum, with in and the accusative
evidence: Vitr. 9 praef.: cum in solium dēscenderet
terms.comment: Vitruvius’s words for Archimedes getting into his bath. A Roman tub was sunk into the floor, so one went down into it; the verb suits a child climbing into a bath as well. solium is the tub (see “bathtub”). Into the water itself, in aquam dēscendere.

evidence: Vitr. 9 praef.: exiluit gaudiō mōtus dē soliō
terms.comment: Archimedes again, leaping out of the bath for joy. Of simply getting out, ē soliō exīre (see the examples); of the baths as a place, Cicero’s ē balineō exīre.

phrases.latin: Aquam prius manū temptā; fortasse nimis calida est.
phrases.english: Test the water with your hand first; it may be too hot.

phrases.latin: Agedum, ē soliō exī; aqua jam frīget.
phrases.english: Come on, out of the bath; the water’s getting cold.

phrases.latin: cum in solium dēscenderet, animadvertit, quantum corporis suī in eō īnsidēret, tantum aquae extrā solium effluere
phrases.english: as he got into the bath he noticed that as much water ran out over the edge as there was of his body sitting in it

phrases.latin: nōn est morātus, sed exiluit gaudiō mōtus dē soliō
phrases.english: he did not wait, but leapt out of the bath for joy

phrases.latin: conjiciāmus nōs in balneum, meō perīculō, nōn paenitēbit. Sīc calet tanquam furnus.
phrases.english: let’s jump into the bath; take my word, you won’t be sorry. It’s as hot as an oven.

phrases.latin: quās litterās cum ē balineō exīssem accēpī
phrases.english: a letter which I received when I had come out of the bath

sources: Lewis & Short: solium · Lewis & Short: descendo · Lewis & Short: exsilio
